answers.question: Global temperature outcome by 2100
answers.answer: Net Zero 2050: 1.6°C by 2050, reducing to 1.4°C by 2100. Delayed Transition: 1.7°C by 2050, reducing to 1.6°C by 2100. Current Policies (Hot House World): 2°C by 2050 and more than 3°C by 2100. A baseline of 1.1°C (current warming) was also used.
answers.evidence: "limit global warming to 1.6°C in 2050 and reducing to 1.4°C by 2100 ... limit global warming to 1.7°C in 2050 and reducing to 1.6°C by 2100 ... resulting in 2°C global warming by 2050 and more than 3°C by 2100"
answers.location_hint: Climate-Related Disclosures p.2; Annual Report p.24
answers.notes: No temperature overshoot language used. The 1.5°C and 3.0°C labels used in the entity-level risk assessment correspond to the Orderly/Disorderly and Hothouse World scenarios respectively.
answers.ani_notes: 1.4oC by 2100 (limited to 1.6oC in 2050) 1.6oC by 2100 (limited to 1.7oC in 2050) 3oC by 2100 (2oC by 2050)

answers.question: Historic climate impacts
answers.answer: Yes — the document describes observed impacts including: increased insurance premiums following climate-related events in NZ, team members in Hastings, Napier, Gisborne and parts of Auckland being affected by severe weather events, and Cyclone Gabrielle (though it did not significantly impact operations directly).
answers.evidence: "Although we have started to feel the transitional impacts of climate change on our business relating to increased legislation (specifically the newly introduced NZ Climate related disclosures) and have seen an increase in insurance premiums off the back of climate-related events occurring in NZ, we have been fortunate that the physical impacts experienced by our business have not significantly impacted operations. We are cognisant some of our team members particularly in Hastings, Napier, Gisborne and parts of Auckland felt the impacts of the severe weather events earlier in the year"
answers.location_hint: Climate-Related Disclosures p.2; Annual Report p.24
answers.notes: Also references Cyclone Gabrielle: "Although Cyclone Gabrielle did not significantly impact us directly, it reinforced our responsibility as an active community member to play a crucial role in addressing future climate challenges." (Annual Report p.15)
answers.ani_notes: We are cognisant some of our team members particularly in Hastings, Napier, Gisborne and parts of Auckland felt the impacts of the severe weather events earlier in the year and we are proud of how our Management team responded to provide support to those impacted, and the way in which our team members worked to ensure our impacted stores could remain open. This year our priority has been on ensuring our business continues to develop an understanding of the risks and opportunities climate change presents

answers.question: Direct and indirect physical climate risks
answers.evidence: "The scope of the climate-risk assessment was Briscoe Group Support Office, our Briscoes Homeware and Rebel Sport store networks across Aotearoa New Zealand and our distribution centres. Consideration was also given to the wider value chain (our suppliers and distribution networks) as they have been, and will continue to be, affected by physical changes to the climate." Direct risks include store closures, building damage, and team/customer access. Indirect risks include: "Impact of a changing climate on the availability of raw materials for our suppliers" and "A main international port is affected (e.g. by storms/or floods). Unable to get goods to New Zealand."
answers.location_hint: Climate-Related Disclosures p.3–5; Annual Report p.25–27
answers.notes: Direct physical risks: storm/flood damage to stores and distribution centres, team member safety, customer access. Indirect physical risks: supplier raw material availability, international port disruption, global supply chain disruption, shipping availability decline.
